title: Coral Reefs of the Red Sea
summary: Coral reefs in the Red Sea are living homes for sea creatures, and they need protection from heat and pollution.
poll: Protecting coral reefs is a job for everyone, not only for scientists.

versions.title: Coral Reefs of the Red Sea
versions.text:
A coral reef may look like a heap of rocks. But it is full of life. Corals are not rocks. They are not plants. They are small animals!

Each coral is soft. It builds a hard cup. Lots of them live side by side. Their cups stack up. In time, they make a reef.

Small things live in each one. They use the sun to make food. They share the food. They give the coral its color, too.

A reef is a home for fish and crabs. Fish hide in its cracks. They find food there.

The Red Sea has lots of reefs. It is warm. Some of its corals can stand a lot of heat. That much heat would hurt corals in some seas.

But reefs are in danger. Some years the sea gets too hot for too long. Then corals push out the small things. They turn white. This is called bleaching. Trash can hurt reefs too.

You can help. Do not touch corals. Keep trash out of the sea. We all must protect reefs.

But reefs are in danger. Some years the sea stays too hot for too long. Then corals push out the tiny living things. Then the corals turn white. This is called bleaching. Trash and dirty water can hurt reefs too.

versions.title: Coral Reefs of the Red Sea
versions.text:
A coral reef may look like a pile of bright rocks from a boat. Under the water, it is full of life. Corals are not rocks. They are not plants. They are tiny animals!

Each coral is soft. It is only a few millimeters wide. It builds a hard, stony cup around its body. The cup keeps it safe. Thousands of corals live together. Old ones die. New ones grow on top of their cups. Over hundreds of years, the cups pile up into a huge reef.

Tiny living things called algae live inside each coral. They use sunlight to make food. They share most of it with the coral. They also give the coral its bright colors.

A reef is a busy home for fish, crabs, turtles, and more. They hide from danger in its holes and cracks. They also find lots of food there.

The Red Sea has some of the longest reefs in the world. Many are along the coast of Saudi Arabia. The water is warm and salty. Some Red Sea corals can stand a lot of heat. Scientists found that this heat would harm corals in other seas.

Still, reefs are in danger. Sometimes the sea stays too hot for too long. Then corals push out their algae. Then the corals turn white. This is called bleaching. Trash and dirty water can also harm reefs.

People can help. Divers should never touch or stand on corals. Boats can tie up to floats. Then they do not drop anchors on reefs. We can all keep trash out of the sea. Together, we can protect the reefs.

versions.title: Coral Reefs of the Red Sea
versions.text:
From a boat, a coral reef may look like a pile of colorful rocks. Under the water, however, it is full of life. Corals are not rocks. They are not plants. They are tiny animals related to jellyfish!

Each coral animal is called a polyp. It is soft and only a few millimeters wide. To protect itself, it builds a hard, stony cup around its body. Thousands of polyps live together in a group. Old polyps die. New ones grow on top of their cups. Over hundreds of years, the cups pile up into a giant reef.

Tiny living things called algae live inside each polyp. They use sunlight to make food. They share most of it with the coral. In return, the coral gives them a safe place to live. The algae also give corals their bright colors.

A reef is a busy home for fish, crabs, sea turtles, and many other sea creatures. They hide from danger in its holes and cracks. They find plenty of food there.

The Red Sea has some of the longest reefs on Earth. Many lie along the coast of Saudi Arabia. Its water is warm and very salty. Scientists have found that some Red Sea corals can survive heat that would harm corals in many other oceans.

Even so, reefs are in danger. Sometimes the sea stays too hot for too long. Then corals push out their algae. Without the algae, the corals turn white. This is called bleaching. If the heat lasts, the corals can starve and die. Trash and dirty water can also harm reefs.

People are working to help. Divers should never touch or stand on corals. Boats can tie up to floats instead of dropping heavy anchors. Everyone can keep trash out of the sea. Together, we can protect the reefs.

From a boat, a coral reef may look like a pile of colorful rocks, but under the water it is bursting with life. Corals are neither rocks nor plants. They are tiny animals, closely related to jellyfish and sea anemones.

Each coral animal, called a polyp, is soft and usually only a few millimeters wide. To protect its delicate body, a polyp builds a hard, stony skeleton beneath it. Thousands of polyps live joined together in a colony. When old polyps die, new ones grow on top of their skeletons, and over hundreds of years these layers pile up to form a massive reef.

Tiny living things called algae live inside each polyp. The algae use sunlight to make food, and they share most of it with the coral. In return, the coral gives them a safe home. The algae also give corals their brilliant colors.

Although coral reefs cover only a small part of the ocean floor, they are home to about a quarter of all sea creatures. Fish, crabs, and sea turtles shelter in the reef's holes and cracks. Reefs also protect beaches by breaking the force of strong waves.

The Red Sea has some of the longest reefs on Earth, and many of them stretch along the coast of Saudi Arabia. Because few rivers flow into it, its water is warm, salty, and remarkably clear. Scientists have discovered that some Red Sea corals can survive heat that would harm corals in many other oceans.

Even so, these reefs face serious danger. When the sea stays too hot for too long, corals push out their algae and turn white, a process called bleaching. If the heat continues, the corals can starve and die. Pollution, such as plastic waste and dirty water, can also damage reefs.

People are working hard to protect reefs. Some areas have become marine parks with strict rules. Boats tie up to floating buoys instead of dropping heavy anchors, and divers learn never to touch corals. Everyone can help by keeping trash out of the sea.

versions.text:
Seen from a boat, a coral reef may resemble a pile of colorful rocks, but beneath the surface it is bursting with life. Corals are neither rocks nor plants. They are tiny animals, closely related to jellyfish and sea anemones.

Each individual coral animal, called a polyp, is soft and usually only a few millimeters wide. To protect its delicate body, a polyp builds a hard skeleton of limestone beneath it. Thousands of polyps live connected together in a colony. When old polyps die, new ones grow on top of their skeletons, and over hundreds or even thousands of years these layers build up into a massive reef.

Microscopic algae live inside the polyps' bodies. The algae use sunlight to produce food, and they share most of it with the coral. In return, the coral provides them with shelter. The algae are also responsible for the brilliant colors of many corals.

Although coral reefs cover only a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, they support about a quarter of all ocean species. Fish, crabs, and sea turtles shelter in the reef's countless holes and cracks. Reefs also protect coastlines by weakening powerful waves before they reach the shore.

The Red Sea contains some of the longest reef systems on Earth, and many of them stretch along the coast of Saudi Arabia. Because very few rivers flow into it, the sea is warm, salty, and remarkably clear. Scientists have discovered that some Red Sea corals can survive temperatures that would harm corals in many other oceans.

Even so, these reefs face serious danger. When seawater stays unusually hot for weeks, corals expel their algae and turn white, a process called bleaching. If the water cools soon, the algae may return; if the heat continues, the corals can starve. Pollution, including plastic waste and sewage, also damages reefs.

People are working to protect these underwater treasures. Some areas have become marine parks with strict rules. Boats tie up to floating buoys instead of dropping heavy anchors, and divers are trained never to touch corals. Everyone can help by keeping trash out of the sea.

versions.title: Coral Reefs of the Red Sea
versions.text:
Seen from a boat, a coral reef may resemble a heap of colorful stones, but beneath the surface it is one of the most crowded and productive environments on the planet. Corals are neither rocks nor plants. They are tiny animals, closely related to jellyfish and sea anemones.

Each individual coral animal, called a polyp, has a soft, tube-shaped body that is usually only a few millimeters wide, with a ring of stinging tentacles around its mouth. To protect itself, a polyp constructs a hard skeleton of limestone beneath its body. Thousands of genetically identical polyps live connected together in a colony. As old polyps die, new generations grow on top of their skeletons, so that over centuries these layers accumulate into an enormous reef.

Microscopic algae live inside the polyps' tissues in a relationship called symbiosis, in which both partners benefit. The algae use sunlight to manufacture food and share most of it with the coral, while the coral supplies them with shelter and nutrients. These algae also produce the brilliant colors of many corals.

Although coral reefs occupy only a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, they support approximately a quarter of all marine species. Fish, crabs, and sea turtles shelter in the reef's countless crevices, and reefs also protect coastlines by absorbing the energy of powerful waves.

The Red Sea contains some of the longest reef systems on Earth, many of them along the coast of Saudi Arabia. Because very few rivers flow into it, the sea is unusually warm, salty, and transparent. Researchers have discovered that certain Red Sea corals can tolerate temperatures that would seriously harm corals elsewhere, so they hope these corals can teach them how reefs might survive a warming world.

Nevertheless, these reefs face serious threats. When seawater remains unusually hot for weeks, stressed corals expel their algae and turn white, a process known as bleaching. If temperatures fall quickly, the algae may return, but if the heat continues, the corals can starve. Pollution, including plastic waste and sewage, causes further damage.

Governments, scientists, and local communities are working on reef conservation. Some areas have become protected marine parks. Boats use floating moorings instead of anchors, divers are trained never to touch corals, and scientists raise young corals in underwater nurseries to replant damaged areas. Everyone can contribute by keeping trash out of the sea.

versions.title: Coral Reefs of the Red Sea
versions.text:
Observed from a boat, a coral reef may resemble a heap of colorful stones, but beneath the surface it is one of the most crowded and biologically productive environments on the planet. Corals are neither minerals nor plants; they are tiny invertebrate animals, closely related to jellyfish and sea anemones.

Each individual coral animal, called a polyp, has a soft, tube-shaped body that is typically only a few millimeters wide, with a ring of stinging tentacles surrounding its mouth. For protection, a polyp constructs a rigid skeleton of limestone beneath its body. Thousands of genetically identical polyps live connected together in a colony, and as older polyps die, successive generations grow on top of their skeletons, so that over centuries these layers accumulate into an enormous, intricate structure.

Microscopic algae inhabit the polyps' tissues in a relationship called symbiosis, in which both partners benefit. The algae use sunlight to manufacture food through photosynthesis and share most of it with the coral, while the coral supplies them with shelter and essential nutrients. These algae are also responsible for the brilliant pigments of many corals.

Although coral reefs occupy only a minuscule fraction of the ocean floor, they support approximately a quarter of all marine species. Fish, crustaceans, and sea turtles shelter within the reef's countless crevices, and reefs additionally safeguard coastlines by absorbing the energy of powerful waves before they reach the shore.

The Red Sea contains some of the longest reef systems on Earth, many of them stretching along the coast of Saudi Arabia. Because very few rivers drain into it, the sea is exceptionally warm, salty, and transparent, and it shelters a considerable number of species found nowhere else. Researchers have discovered that certain Red Sea corals can tolerate temperatures that would seriously harm corals elsewhere, and they hope these remarkable organisms can reveal how reefs might endure an increasingly warm climate.

Nevertheless, these ecosystems face serious threats. When seawater remains abnormally hot for weeks, stressed corals expel their algae and turn white, a process known as bleaching. If temperatures decline quickly, the algae may gradually return, but if the heat persists, the weakened corals can starve. Pollution, including plastic debris and untreated sewage, inflicts additional damage.

Governments, scientists, and coastal communities are consequently collaborating on reef conservation. Certain areas have been designated as protected marine parks, vessels attach to floating moorings rather than dropping anchors, divers are trained never to touch corals, and scientists cultivate young corals in underwater nurseries to replant damaged sections. Every individual can contribute by preventing trash from reaching the sea.

versions.title: Coral Reefs of the Red Sea
versions.text:
Observed from a boat, a coral reef may resemble a heap of colorful stones scattered haphazardly across the seabed, but beneath the surface it constitutes one of the most crowded and biologically productive environments on the entire planet. Corals are neither minerals nor plants; they are tiny invertebrate animals, closely related to jellyfish and sea anemones, and their apparent stillness conceals an extraordinarily active biological process.

Each individual coral animal, called a polyp, has a soft, tube-shaped body that is typically only a few millimeters wide, with a ring of stinging tentacles surrounding its mouth. For protection against predators and the physical force of waves, a polyp constructs a rigid skeleton of limestone beneath its own body. Thousands of genetically identical polyps live connected together in a single colony, and as older polyps gradually die, successive generations grow directly on top of their predecessors' skeletons, so that over centuries these accumulated layers build into an enormous, intricate limestone structure.

Microscopic algae inhabit the polyps' tissues in a mutually beneficial relationship called symbiosis, in which both partners derive substantial advantage from the arrangement. The algae use sunlight to manufacture food through photosynthesis and subsequently share most of this food with the coral host, while the coral in turn supplies the algae with physical shelter and essential nutrients that they could not easily obtain alone. These resident algae are additionally responsible for the brilliant pigments that give many corals their characteristic and often vivid appearance.

Although coral reefs collectively occupy only a minuscule fraction of the entire ocean floor, they nevertheless support approximately a quarter of all known marine species, an astonishing concentration of biodiversity relative to their physical footprint. Fish, crustaceans, and sea turtles shelter within the reef's countless crevices, finding both refuge from predators and abundant food. Reefs additionally safeguard coastlines by absorbing a substantial portion of the destructive energy carried by powerful waves before those waves ever reach the shore.

The Red Sea contains some of the longest reef systems on Earth, many of them stretching along the coast of Saudi Arabia for considerable distances. Because very few rivers drain into it, the sea itself is exceptionally warm, salty, and transparent, conditions that shelter a considerable number of species found nowhere else on the planet. Researchers have discovered that certain Red Sea corals can tolerate temperatures that would seriously harm corals elsewhere, and they consequently hope these remarkable organisms will eventually reveal how reefs more broadly might endure an increasingly warm global climate.

Nevertheless, these ecosystems face serious and mounting threats. When seawater remains abnormally hot for several consecutive weeks, stressed corals expel their resident algae and turn uniformly white, a dramatic process known as bleaching. If temperatures decline reasonably quickly afterward, the expelled algae may gradually return, but if the underlying heat persists, the weakened corals can eventually starve from the loss of their primary food source. Pollution, including plastic debris and untreated sewage, inflicts additional and compounding damage on these already fragile communities.

Governments, scientists, and coastal communities are consequently collaborating on ambitious reef conservation efforts. Certain areas have been formally designated as protected marine parks, vessels increasingly attach to floating moorings rather than dropping destructive anchors onto living coral, divers are carefully trained never to touch the fragile structures, and scientists cultivate young corals in underwater nurseries in order to replant damaged sections. Every individual, whether near the coast or far from it, can contribute meaningfully by preventing trash from ever reaching the sea.

versions.title: Coral Reefs of the Red Sea
versions.text:
Observed from a boat, a coral reef may resemble a heap of colorful stones scattered haphazardly across the seabed, but beneath the surface it constitutes one of the most crowded and biologically productive environments on the entire planet, rivaling even tropical rainforests in the sheer density of life it sustains. Corals are neither minerals nor plants; they are tiny invertebrate animals, closely related to jellyfish and sea anemones, and their apparent stillness conceals an extraordinarily active, continuous biological process beneath the surface.

Each individual coral animal, called a polyp, has a soft, tube-shaped body that is typically only a few millimeters wide, with a ring of stinging tentacles surrounding its mouth. For protection against predators and the relentless physical force of breaking waves, a polyp constructs a rigid skeleton of limestone beneath its own body. Thousands of genetically identical polyps live connected together within a single colony, and as older polyps gradually die, successive generations grow directly on top of their predecessors' skeletons, so that over centuries these accumulated layers build into an enormous, intricate limestone structure capable of supporting an entire ecosystem.

Microscopic algae inhabit the polyps' tissues in a mutually beneficial relationship called symbiosis, in which both partners derive substantial advantage from their close physiological association. The algae use sunlight to manufacture food through photosynthesis and subsequently share most of this food with the coral host, while the coral in turn supplies the algae with physical shelter and essential nutrients that they could not easily obtain on their own in open water. These resident algae are additionally responsible for the brilliant pigments that give many corals their characteristic and often strikingly vivid appearance, pigments that fade immediately once the algae depart.

Although coral reefs collectively occupy only a minuscule fraction of the entire ocean floor, they nevertheless support approximately a quarter of all known marine species, an astonishing concentration of biodiversity relative to their modest physical footprint. Fish, crustaceans, and sea turtles shelter within the reef's countless crevices, finding both refuge from predators and an abundant, reliable source of food. Reefs additionally safeguard coastlines by absorbing a substantial portion of the destructive energy carried by powerful waves before those waves ever reach the shore, a service that protects coastal communities as much as it protects marine life.

The Red Sea contains some of the longest reef systems on Earth, many of them stretching along the coast of Saudi Arabia for considerable distances. Because very few rivers drain into it, the sea itself is exceptionally warm, salty, and transparent, conditions that shelter a considerable number of species found nowhere else on the planet. Researchers have discovered that certain Red Sea corals can tolerate temperatures that would seriously harm or kill corals elsewhere, and they consequently hope these remarkable organisms will eventually reveal how reefs more broadly might endure an increasingly warm and unpredictable global climate.

Nevertheless, these ecosystems face serious and steadily mounting threats. When seawater remains abnormally hot for several consecutive weeks, stressed corals expel their resident algae and turn uniformly white, a dramatic process known as bleaching that can strip a once-colorful reef of nearly all its visible vibrancy within days. If temperatures decline reasonably quickly afterward, the expelled algae may gradually return and recolonize the coral, but if the underlying heat persists, the weakened corals can eventually starve from the prolonged loss of their primary food source. Pollution, including plastic debris and untreated sewage discharged from coastal settlements, inflicts additional and compounding damage on these already fragile communities.

Governments, scientists, and coastal communities are consequently collaborating on increasingly ambitious reef conservation efforts. Certain areas have been formally designated as protected marine parks with enforceable regulations, vessels increasingly attach to floating moorings rather than dropping destructive anchors directly onto living coral, divers are carefully trained never to touch the fragile structures beneath them, and scientists cultivate young corals in underwater nurseries specifically in order to replant damaged or bleached sections. Every individual, whether living near the coast or far inland, can contribute meaningfully to this effort by preventing trash from ever reaching the sea in the first place.

MID.prompt: Explain how corals and algae depend on each other, and how bleaching breaks this partnership. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained what corals and algae give each other.
I described what happens during bleaching.
I used evidence from the article to support my answer.
MID.modelAnswer: Corals and algae depend on each other in a close partnership. Each coral polyp builds a hard skeleton to protect its soft body, and tiny algae live inside the polyp, using sunlight to make food that they share with the coral. In return, the algae get a safe home and give the coral its bright colors. However, bleaching breaks this partnership when the water stays too hot for too long, because the stressed coral pushes out its algae and turns white. Without the algae's food, the coral can starve, and pollution can make this damage even worse.

HIGH.prompt: Researchers are studying heat-tolerant Red Sea corals. Explain why this research matters for reefs around the world, using evidence about bleaching and conservation from the article.
checklist: I explained why heat-tolerant corals interest researchers.
I connected the research to the threat of bleaching.
I supported my ideas with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: This research matters because Red Sea corals have shown a remarkable ability to tolerate heat that would destroy corals in most other oceans, which makes their symbiosis with algae especially resilient. Normally, when water temperatures rise too high, stressed corals expel their algae in a process called bleaching, and if the heat does not ease, the coral's limestone skeleton is left bare and the animal eventually starves. Because Red Sea corals seem better able to withstand this stress, scientists studying them may discover traits or conditions that could help conservation efforts protect vulnerable reefs elsewhere as ocean temperatures continue rising. In this way, one resilient reef could offer hope for reef ecosystems around the entire world.
